title: Sole Proprietor Versus Corporation
subtitle: Choose a structure that fits your work and the money you need at home.

blocks.text: Choosing a business structure can feel like buying a filing cabinet before you know what goes in it. Start with the work you will do, the risks it brings and the cash you need to live on.
Give your choice a reason.
blocks.detail: You will be able to explain why a structure fits your work today, instead of picking it because the name sounds impressive.
blocks.extra: Section 03 lays the two side by side, using the same business.

sections.title: Who owns the business and its money?

blocks.text: The CRA says a sole proprietor is one owner with no separate legal status. That owner carries the business risk and reports net business income on a personal T1 tax return. Personal savings and property can be at risk.

Corporations Canada describes a corporation as a separate legal person. Shareholders own the shares, and the company’s money belongs to the company. One person can still run the daily work but must respect that line.
Neither choice is a prize for reaching a certain sales number. This lesson helps you compare your facts before you choose. It does not replace advice on your own legal and tax situation.

Picture a home-organizing service with one owner. Keep its jobs, prices and clients the same while you compare the two structures. If you don’t, you may end up comparing a tiny service with a much bigger company.

items.title: Ownership and control: will you work alone, or invite another owner? If considering shares, discuss who can make which decisions.
items.text: Ownership and control: will you work alone, or bring in another owner? If shares come into it, agree who can make which decisions.

items.title: Risk: could a job damage property, expose private records, or involve disputed instructions? List the actual work before asking about protection.
items.text: Risk: could a job damage property, expose private papers or lead to a dispute about instructions? List the real tasks before you ask about protection.

items.title: Administration: price the bookkeeping, tax preparation, registry obligations, and your own time for each option.
items.text: Running costs: price the bookkeeping, tax filing, registry filings and your own time for each option.

items.title: Cash: how much must reach your household, and how much could stay available for business plans?
items.text: Cash: how much must reach your household each month, and how much could stay in the business for future plans?

blocks.text: The main differences at a glance

items.title: TAX ON PROFIT
items.text: Sole proprietor: all profit is added to your personal income and taxed at your personal rates. Corporation: profit is taxed in the company first. A small Canadian-controlled private company can pay a lower federal rate of 9% on its first $500,000 of active business income, plus the provincial rate. You pay personal tax again when you take money out.

items.title: CPP
items.text: Sole proprietor: you pay both halves of CPP on your profit. Corporation: a salary means the company runs payroll and both shares of CPP are paid. Dividends carry no CPP, which lowers what you pay now and your pension later.

items.title: EARLY LOSSES
items.text: Sole proprietor: a business loss can lower the tax on your other income, such as a job, in the same year. Corporation: the loss stays in the company and can only be used against its own profits.

items.title: SET-UP AND UPKEEP
items.text: Sole proprietor: little or no set-up cost. Corporation: a filing fee ($200 federally), a yearly registry return, a T2 return and usually higher accounting fees every year.

blocks.text: A business name does not settle risk. A clear contract should say what you will handle, what needs the client’s approval and what is outside the service.

The CRA says corporations file a T2 tax return every year. Corporations Canada adds company records and a yearly registry return, which is separate from tax. These tasks belong in the comparison, even in a quiet year.

If you incorporate, wages and dividends are taxed in different ways. The CRA treats pay to an employee differently from benefits and dividends paid to a shareholder. If the company pays your personal bills, that can count as a taxable benefit. Plan how you will be paid before you move any money.
A lower company tax rate alone cannot show your total result. Ask an accountant to compare company tax, your personal tax, how you take pay and the running costs, all using the same income.

items.title: “Sole proprietors have no paperwork.”
items.text: A simpler structure still needs good records. Keep invoices and expenses organized, and check the tax accounts, registrations and permits your work requires.

blocks.text: Some regulated professions have special rules about who can own the business or how it is set up. If that sounds like your work, check with your regulator and province before you narrow the choice.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: Luc’s two folders

blocks.text: Luc’s two folders
paragraphs: Luc lived in Moncton and ran a home-organizing service. He wanted it to help pay the household bills. He made two folders, one for each structure. He hoped a tidy desk would give him a tidy answer.

A client asked him to clear a packed storage room and haul away the things she didn’t want. While he looked over the job, Luc spotted a box marked “family papers” next to the donation pile. Suddenly the risk was about a real task, not a business title.

He paused the booking and asked which items the client would approve for removal. He also called an insurance adviser about the work. A friend said incorporating would make the whole worry go away. Luc wanted to know which risks would stay.

Luc wrote down what his service covered and what his household needed each month. He asked for the yearly cost of each structure and an accountant’s comparison. For now, he chose to stay a sole proprietor. He turned down removal work until his contract and insurance were checked.

Then a property manager offered regular visits across several units. Luc could have treated it as the answer to his income hopes. But the bigger job changed his plan. He asked to see the contract before he promised a start date.

The offer stayed under review, and no income was promised. Luc set a date to look at incorporating again before taking on bigger work. His two folders now held facts and questions, which beat matching labels by a mile.

blocks.text: Luc’s choice is one made-up outcome. Another owner with different contracts, partners or savings could sensibly incorporate from the start.
Make the next decision easier.
blocks.detail: A written reason and a review point help you respond fast when a new contract changes your risks or cash needs.
blocks.extra: Section 05 helps you write that one-page brief.

blocks.text: Use this exercise to prepare for a useful talk with an adviser. It is a decision brief, not a filing checklist. Put both structures on one page and note what supports each choice.
First, write the working facts

For Luc’s small made-up service, write: one owner; sorting with the client present; nothing removed without approval; no heavy moving. Then list the bigger contract on its own. Do not let possible future work slip in as if it were a promise.
Ask an insurance adviser about your exact tasks and what is not covered, under either structure. Ask a lawyer which contract terms and duties need attention.
Next, test the cash available

Made-up monthly example, sales tax left out: $5,000 collected from clients minus $1,500 in business costs leaves $3,500 before income tax, owner pay and any extra structure costs. If Luc needs $2,800 for his household, only $700 is left before those other items.

That $700 is not spare money for growth or proof of a tax saving. Ask the accountant how much can safely reach the household under each option, and what is left after all tax and running costs. Test a slow month too. Unpaid invoices do not buy groceries.
Compare the same service and the same household need. Leaving money in a company may help future plans, but it does not turn that money into a personal spending account.
Finish with a reason and a trigger

Write the structure you prefer for now, your strongest reason and one fact that still needs checking. Add a trigger, such as a second owner or a bigger contract, that would send you back to the comparison.

items.title: “Incorporation removes all personal liability.”
items.text: The CRA warns that personal guarantees and some director duties can still put your own money at risk.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Bring your scope, your cash estimate and your real contract questions to the adviser. “What changes if I take this job?” is easier to answer than “Which structure is best?”
Quick Check

items.title: Does corporate money belong directly to its shareholder?
items.text: Keep business ownership and company money distinct.

items.title: In the example, is the remaining $700 already available for business growth?
items.text: Tax and extra structure costs still need review.

items.title: What should change when the proposed work becomes wider?
items.detail: Review the scope, protection, cash estimate, and structure decision before accepting.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: An organizer expects $3,500 before tax and needs $2,800 at home. What should guide the structure comparison? A. A tax rate alone. · B. Household cash after tax and structure costs. · C. The shortest business name.
items.text: Money needed at home matters; the example’s $700 is still before tax and extra costs.

items.title: A new client requests heavy moving outside the planned service. What is the sound next step? A. Review scope, coverage, and responsibilities. · B. Assume incorporation covers it. · C. Accept before reading the contract.
items.text: A changed task requires a fresh review before a promise to the client.

items.title: An owner incorporates an existing service. What should they expect? A. Every account transfers automatically. · B. Only the invoice logo changes. · C. Review the new business number, accounts, contracts, and assets.
items.text: CRA explains that a structure change can require new accounts. Get advice on tax effects and transferring contracts, assets, and banking arrangements.

items.title: Written response: Give one reason for your current preferred structure and one fact that would make you review it.
items.text: I am comparing a sole proprietorship for my narrow service; I will review it before signing a contract covering several properties.

blocks.text: Choose from your actual work, cash needs, and ongoing obligations. Write down what could change the decision, and review that fact before taking on new work.
Use the work you do now, not a hoped-for best year. If you have not started, describe the service you plan to offer and mark any facts you still need to check.

Finish your one-page decision brief. Include the structure you are leaning toward, your reason, and one open question with a next step and a review date. Use it to book a focused talk with a lawyer, insurance adviser or accountant.

items.title: Sole proprietor
items.text: One person who owns a business that is not incorporated.

items.title: Corporation
items.text: A separate legal person with its own money and duties.

items.title: Shareholder
items.text: Someone who owns shares in a corporation.

items.title: Personal guarantee
items.text: Your personal promise to repay a set business debt.

items.title: Dividend
items.text: A payment to shareholders based on the shares they own.

items.title: Decision brief
items.text: Your written facts, choice, reason and review point.
